opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to what kind of layer the inference engine is. It sits right in the middle of the AI stack. Below it you have many kinds of hardware: NVIDIA GPUs, AMD, TPUs, and a growing number of domestic and specialized accelerators. Above it you have a rapidly changing set of models, with new architectures and new attention variants, mixture-of-experts, long context, multimodality. Every time something changes on either side, the inference engine has to adapt. No single company can keep up with all of that alone.

When it's open source, the model developers can contribute support for their own models, often on day zero of a release. Hardware vendors can contribute their own backends and kernels. Researchers can try new scheduling or caching ideas directly in a real system instead of a toy prototype. So the engine becomes a kind of common meeting point. Everyone puts in a little and everyone gets much more back. That network effect is really the core value, and it only exists if the project is open.

There's also a more personal reason. I came from academia, and I've always felt that infrastructure like this should be a public good, a bit like Linux or PyTorch. If serving large models efficiently is locked inside a few big companies, then the cost of using AI stays high and the power stays concentrated. If it's open, a small startup, a university lab, or a developer in any country can deploy a strong model at a reasonable cost. Lowering that barrier matters a lot to me.

And honestly, open source keeps us honest technically. Our code is out there, people benchmark it, people find bugs, people complain loudly on GitHub. That pressure is uncomfortable sometimes, but it makes the system much better and much more reliable than something built behind closed doors.

Of course, keeping it open isn't free. Maintaining a project with so many contributors, reviewing code, keeping the architecture clean while it grows really fast, all of that is hard work. But I believe that in the long run, the open approach is the one that wins for this layer, and it's the one that's best for the whole ecosystem.

r001.rationale: The response discusses open source benefits and the difficulty of maintaining it, but never identifies founding a company to pursue a closed-source inference engine as an available alternative.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the simplest answer is that inference is becoming infrastructure, and infrastructure should not belong to any single company.

When I started working on vLLM, the model layer was already getting more open. Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, Mistral, all of these weights were being released, and people could download them and run them. But a model file on disk is not a product. You need a system that takes that model and actually serves it, efficiently, to many users at once, with good latency, good throughput, on whatever hardware you happen to have. That piece in the middle is the inference engine. If that piece is closed, then the openness of the model is a bit of an illusion. You would have open weights, but you could only really use them well through someone else's proprietary stack, and that company would effectively decide what hardware works, what models get supported first, and what the pricing looks like.

The second reason is more practical. The space is moving incredibly fast. Every few weeks there is a new attention variant, a new quantization scheme, a new model architecture, a new chip. No single team, no matter how talented, can keep up with all of that. With vLLM, when a new model comes out, very often the model team themselves contributes the support, sometimes before the model is even publicly announced. Hardware vendors contribute their own backends. Researchers who invent a new scheduling idea or a new kernel can land it directly. That kind of velocity simply does not happen behind closed doors. Open source is not a charity thing for us. It is the fastest way to build the best system.

And the third reason is trust. Inference is where the model actually meets the user. If people are going to deploy these systems in hospitals, in banks, in their own data centers, they need to be able to read the code, audit it, fix it, and run it themselves without asking permission. I came from an academic background, and I think the research community also benefits enormously from having a strong open baseline. Many papers now evaluate against vLLM or build on top of it. That would be impossible if it were a black box.

Of course there are costs. Maintaining a popular open source project is exhausting. You are reviewing contributions from hundreds of people with different priorities, and you have to make decisions about what goes in and what does not. But every time I see someone in a small startup or a university lab run a frontier model on a couple of GPUs because of our work, I feel that this is the right trade-off. The whole point is that the ability to run these models should be a public good, not a moat.

r001.rationale: The response argues that inference infrastructure should not belong to one company, but it does not identify founding their own company as an available alternative for building a closed-source inference engine.

astra-6.text:
For me, an inference engine is a fundamental part of the infrastructure for using AI. Keeping it open source means people can understand how it works, adapt it to their needs, and improve it together. They don’t have to depend entirely on one company’s decisions.

It also matters because inference has so many different workloads and hardware environments. No single team can anticipate all of them. When users can inspect the code, report problems, and contribute improvements, we can build something more useful together. That’s why I see open source as more than releasing code—it’s a way to share ownership of the infrastructure.

r001.rationale: The response explains reasons for keeping the inference engine open source but does not identify founding their own company as an alternative for pursuing a closed-source engine.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, keeping an inference engine open source is about trust and shared progress. It sits at a critical point between a model and the people using it. Developers should be able to understand how it works, investigate problems, and adapt it to their needs.

There’s also so much variety in models, hardware, and workloads that no single team can anticipate everything. With open source, someone can find a bottleneck, contribute an improvement, and make that improvement available to everyone. That’s the kind of collaboration I want to support.

r001.rationale: The response discusses trust, shared progress, and collaboration in open source, but does not identify founding a company as an alternative for pursuing a closed-source inference engine.
